entities.summary:
Scopas, an eminent Greek sculptor and architect active in the mid-4th century BCE, notably during the transition from the Late Classical to the early Hellenistic periods, profoundly reshaped the aesthetic landscape of ancient Greece. Hailing from Paros, a renowned source of fine marble, his artistic output was characterized by an intense expressiveness and mastery of drapery. This dynamic style broke from the serene idealism of earlier High Classical masters like Phidias, making him a pivotal figure in the evolution of Greek art across the Peloponnese and Asia Minor.

Among Scopas's most celebrated sculptural achievements are his contributions to the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, where he sculpted significant portions of the frieze depicting the Gigantomachy and Amazonomachy around 353-350 BCE. His statue of Meleager, known through numerous Roman copies, exemplifies his ability to convey profound pathos and physical tension. He also created cult statues, such as the copper Aphrodite for Samothrace and the head of the goddess Hygieia, daughter of Asclepius, for Tegea. Furthermore, Scopas served as the architect for the Temple of Athena Alea at Tegea, rebuilding it after a fire in 395 BCE, integrating his sculptural prowess directly into the architectural fabric of sacred spaces.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Scopas was a pivotal figure in the transition from Classical to Hellenistic Greek art, introducing a dynamic, emotional style that profoundly influenced later sculptors and left an indelible mark on monumental projects like the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus.
